claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of a high-entropy alloy is governed by the dynamic balance between mechanical passive-film removal and electrochemical repassivation.
Sliding wear continuously disrupts the metastable passive oxide layer.
When the passive film is disrupted by sliding, net degradation is primarily controlled by the oxide reformation rate.
The initial high-entropy alloy naturally develops a passive oxide film.
The passive film is rich in passivating elements such as Cr or Al.
Heat treatment, grain refinement, or a slight alloying adjustment can enhance passive-film repassivation kinetics.
Passive-film stability, thickness, and adherence are influenced by grain size and defect density.
Passive-film stability, thickness, and adherence are influenced by elemental distribution.
Faster electrochemical repassivation can restore the protective film before excessive metal exposure occurs.
The competition between film disruption and repassivation governs the corrosion rate.
The competition between film disruption and repassivation governs wear volume.
Relative to a matched alloy with slower repassivation, a modified alloy with enhanced oxide reformation will have lower total degradation.
The modified alloy will develop a shallower wear track than the coarser-grained baseline.
The modified alloy will show a lower corrosion current or less pit formation than the baseline.
The predicted improvement should hold in oxidizing electrolytes that promote passive-oxide formation.
The predicted improvement should hold only when wear does not overwhelm the film-reformation capacity.
The predicted improvement may fail under extremely aggressive mechanical wear.
The predicted improvement may fail in inert environments where oxide formation is minimal.
